pr_title: Fix bad case-insensitive ASCII equality check
pr_body:
Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/45889. There was an edge case where the characters ``'`'`` and `'@'` would inadvertently compare as equal under _OrdinalIgnoreCase_. This PR also introduces a unit test to run through all combinations of ASCII chars to look for other edge cases, and it looks like this was the only edge case.

My AMD-based dev box is reporting a tiny perf improvement: maybe 1 cycle or so. I'm not able to measure this with much accuracy, so I'd depend on the perf lab to let us know if something has gone horribly wrong. Since we're reducing the overall code size I wouldn't expect throughput to regress.

This will need to be backported to 5.x and 3.x.
pr_comments: FYI to reviewers - the diff is a few dozen lines, but that's mostly because I rewrote the comments in the code to clarify exactly what the bit twiddling accomplishes. The fix itself is only a half dozen lines or so, duplicated across 4 methods.

Latest iteration only changes the unit test. Easiest way to review the single-commit delta is to ignore whitespace changes: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/45928/commits/7380c458619d0dbeefb04a07d88c0453ad05ab0e?diff=unified&w=1
@GrabYourPitchforks a general question: have you tried to vectorize `Ordinal.EqualsIgnoreCase` ? I see it's currently "vectorized" via GP registers or it doesn't make sense?

NIT: would be nice to address Ben's feedback https://github.com/dotnet/coreclr/pull/20734#discussion_r230545414
(`UInt32OrdinalIgnoreCaseAscii` -> `UInt32OrdinalIgnoreCaseAsciiEqauls`) but I guess it's better to keep as is for less painful backport to 3.1 and 5.0.

@EgorBo We measured it a while back. Vectorization really only provides a benefit when we're talking about long-ish inputs (over a few dozen chars). Since typical inputs to this method are on the order of ~10 chars max, using non-vectorized code incurred less overhead than using vectorized code and had better perf characteristics.
+ @adamsitnik, because you like weird bit twiddling tricks :)

@GrabYourPitchforks backporting to release/5.0 failed, the patch most likely resulted in conflicts:

issue_context.title: string Equals StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase bug with @ and ` characters
comments:
Tagging subscribers to this area: @tarekgh, @safern, @krwq See info in area-owners.md if you want to be subscribed.
Issue Details
### Description var atsymbol = "@a"; var backtick = "`a"; // returns false as expected Console.WriteLine($"Is {atsymbol} equal to {backtick}: {atsymbol.Equals(backtick, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)}"); // returns true which is very wrong Console.WriteLine($"Is {backtick} equal to {atsymbol}: {backtick.Equals(atsymbol, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)}"); ### Configuration * Which version of .NET is the code running on? ** Visual Studio Project says: netcoreapp3.1 ** dotnet --version = 3.1.401 * What OS and version, and what distro if applicable? windows 10 * What is the architecture (x64, x86, ARM, ARM64)? x64 * Do you know whether it is specific to that configuration? No
Author: matroberts
Assignees: -
Labels: `area-System.Globalization`, `untriaged`
Milestone: -

The problem seems in `UInt32OrdinalIgnoreCaseAscii` (same for `UInt64OrdinalIgnoreCaseAscii`) from https://github.com/dotnet/coreclr/pull/20734 e.g.:
```csharp
UInt32OrdinalIgnoreCaseAscii('@', '`'); // false
UInt32OrdinalIgnoreCaseAscii('`', '@'); // true
```
I guess that check for "is upper case" (0x20 bit) is a bit incorrect.

```
'a' 01100001
'A' 01000001
'@' 01000000
'`' 01100000
      ^
```
2.1 is fine; 3.1 and later are not.
Found the issue, trying to figure out how to fix it without harming perf, given how absurdly hot this code path is.

Assuming _valA_ is the long tail of the operation...

Current codegen:

```asm
xor valB, valA
lea tmp, [valA + CONST]
or valA, CONST
add valA, CONST
or valA, tmp  ; dependency on tmp (may stall)
shr valA, 2
or valA, CONST
test valA, valB  ; dependency on valB
```

With proposed fix (still under test):

```asm
xor valB, valA
shl valB, 2  ; parallelize with arithmetic operations below
add valA, CONST
or valA, CONST
add valA, CONST
or valA, CONST
test valA, valB  ; dependency on valB, latency 1 shl operation should *just* be finishing
```

This should end up being a bit more efficient due to a shorter chain on _valA_ and the lack of a possibly-stalling dependency on _tmp_. In fact, _tmp_ is gone entirely, which should also make the register allocator happier.

Still need to unit test + perf test.
Fixing the bug _and_ making it faster - nice!
Yeah, definitely a servicing candidate. I'll prep the 3.1 servicing email next week since there's no rush.
removing 'servicing consider' as that goes on PRs
This was backported to 3.1 via https://github.com/dotnet/coreclr/pull/28118. Closing since I believe this servicing event is resolved.
